en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of the Elder Mahābala, Scroll One.
Translated by Imperial Decree by the Dharma Master of the Western Heaven,
Bestowed Purple Robe Śramaṇa Jñānaśrī, and others during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats.

With all outflows extinguished and freed from the bonds of affliction, their minds were well-liberated and their wisdom well-liberated; like great dragon kings, they manifested through divine transformations, accomplishing all that was to be done without exception; having cast off the heavy burden and attained their own welfare, their mental faculties were liberated and they possessed mastery over all phenomena, being fully capable of practicing the conduct that reaches the further shore.
Furthermore, there was the Venerable Ānanda, preeminent among those of great learning and sharp faculties;
and there were also five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had attained various dhāraṇīs and dwelt in samādhi, all together within the assembly.
At that time, there was a householder in the great city of Śrāvastī named Mahābala, who was endowed with a perfect physical appearance and whose fame was heard afar.

This householder’s family was immensely wealthy, possessing vast quantities of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and great mani-jewels—wondrous and precious treasures that filled every storehouse. His wealth, grain, and all manner of utensils for enjoyment were beyond counting, and he had everything he desired in full abundance.

Whatever he required was never lacking; his capital and interest circulated throughout other countries so that there was no place where they were not present. His various laborers, slaves, servants, attendants, and officials, as well as his elephants, horses, and carriages, were likewise numerous.

The site where the elder resided was magnificent and elegant, featuring double gates, towers, and pavilions; its halls, chambers, and dwellings were adorned with various jewels whose radiance illuminated one another. Its gardens and ponds abounded in rare and wondrous flowers and fruits, and its manifold adornments were beyond compare. The courtesans and musical performances were all of the highest excellence, surpassing all except those of the king. Within this setting, the elder enjoyed the utmost pleasure, uninterrupted throughout the six periods of day and night.
At that time, the Elder had five hundred other elders as his assistants; they were in charge of precious jewels and guarded the storehouses containing the necessities of life.
Then, at one moment, the Elder Mahābala’s roots of goodness suddenly matured and a realization arose in his mind, whereupon he thought to himself:

"This floating world is not solid, like what is seen in a dream; all forms and appearances ultimately end in decay and extinction. This body, too, is by nature fundamentally empty and likewise subject to ruin. The causes of the pleasures of the five desires produce the fruits of increasing suffering; the masses are blind and deluded, with no time of liberation in sight."
At that very moment, he summoned all the elders to assemble and sit together, and addressed the multitude:

"All of you should be silent and listen attentively. All phenomena arise from the gathering of conditions and perish when conditions disperse; their essential nature is not real, for they ultimately end in decay and ruin. Sentient beings give rise to various discriminations through deluded thoughts, clinging to the existence of a self and one's kin. Failing to understand impermanence—the momentary arising and ceasing—they find their wealth and dwellings turning into the property of others. Out of foolish arrogance, they create the causes for the five realms of existence; once karmic bonds are formed, they undergo various disparate retributions. It is easy to fall into the evil paths, but difficult to be born in the happy realms."
"You should all know that a human body is difficult to obtain; that one can now, even for a single moment, give rise to right mindfulness is what is called difficult.

You elders, furthermore, you are able to know that those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world and are difficult to encounter; that having been born in a Buddha-land, your faith does not regress—this too is difficult."
To give rise to a mind of faith and aspiration toward the Buddha’s true teaching, and to renounce the secular world out of weary detachment and become a monk, is difficult.
Although one has become a monk, to be able to cultivate the pure brahmacarya of a bhikṣu and eliminate adverse conditions is even more difficult.
To practice various forms of dhyāna with diligent application day and night, remaining far removed from distraction, is also difficult.
To possess a nature that is sharp and wise, such that one is well able to discern the authenticity or falsity of all phenomena, is likewise difficult.
Now, to have attained human birth and further encountered a virtuous king, who brings all strife to rest and establishes one in a state of peace and happiness, is also exceedingly difficult.
If sentient beings cultivate various merits and give rise to a mind directed toward the land of the Tathāgata with constant firmness, that too is difficult.

"Furthermore, it is difficult for sentient beings to use skillful means and eloquent speech to exhort various spiritual friends to cultivate meritorious deeds, go to the presence of the Buddha, and approach him to make offerings."

If there are sentient beings who distance themselves from poverty, meagerness, and ignorance; who possess abundant merit and wisdom and are born in the Buddha-lands; and who, among the multitudes, are able to perform various kinds of adorned Buddha-works—this indeed is difficult.

If there are sentient beings who, through diligence and the observance of precepts, seek liberation by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle; seek liberation by means of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; or seek liberation by means of the Unsurpassed Vehicle—this is truly difficult.
At that time, after the elder Mahābala had spoken of these three vehicles and various matters, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"You should give rise to awakening according to what I have said, thoroughly understanding that the characteristics of form are not solid."
At that time, five hundred elders among those seated there heard this account and were like people intoxicated by wine, utterly lacking any awakening.
Then, one elder from within the assembly rose from his seat and addressed the elder Mahābala, saying:
"We all now have doubts; what are the so-called Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Anuttarayāna vehicles?"
"What are the physical forms and the objects of the five sensual pleasures found in the world? Their essential nature is not solid, arising and ceasing in every moment.
Please explain this to us again in detail; we wish to hear it with great longing."
At that time, the elder Mahābala addressed that elder and the assembly, saying:

"In this great city of Śrāvastī, within the Jeta Grove at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, there is the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He is endowed with the three knowledges (trividyā), the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa); he is fully possessed of the ten powers (daśabala), the four fearlessnesses (caturvaiśāradya), and the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇikadharma). He is named the All-Knowing One (sarvajña) and is titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans."
In that assembly, he shall preach the Dharma for the multitude and resolve their web of doubts.
We, together with you all, should go there in unison to approach and make offerings to him, and inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such wondrous Dharma.

When the five hundred elders heard these words, each was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation. Carrying exquisite incense, flowers, and various kinds of rare jewels, they went together with the elder Mahābala to the place where the Buddha was. They circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated at his feet, and after making offerings with reverence, singing hymns and offering praises, they withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the roots of goodness of those elders and others had matured and they were capable of receiving the sublime Dharma, addressed the elder Mahābala and the five hundred elders, saying:
"For what reason have you come here?"

At that time, there was an elder among the assembly who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, praised the World-Honored One, saying:

"We previously heard the skillful instruction of the Elder Mahābala, who said that the worldly forms, the five desires, and the implements of pleasure are by nature not solid or real, but ultimately end in decay and extinction—and so on at length. Now, this human body is extremely difficult to obtain; furthermore, if one can, for even a single kṣaṇa, give rise to right mindfulness and sever the mind of false delusion, that too is difficult."
The appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world is difficult to encounter; once born in a Buddha-land, it is likewise difficult to possess faith.

To give rise to a mind of faith and inclination toward the true teaching of the Buddha, and to feel weary of and detached from the mundane world while aspiring to leave the household life—this too is difficult.
Although one has left the household life, to be able to cultivate the pure brahmacarya of a bhikṣu and extinguish all evil conditions is difficult.
To practice various dhyānas with diligent effort day and night, remaining far removed from distraction, is likewise difficult.
"If one possesses a nature that is sharp and wise, such that one is well able to discern the truth and falsehood of all phenomena, this is indeed difficult.
Now, to have attained human birth and further encountered a virtuous king, who brings an end to all strife and establishes one in a state of peace and happiness—this too is exceedingly difficult."
If sentient beings cultivate various merits and are born in the land of the Tathāgata, this too is difficult.

Furthermore, if sentient beings can, through skillful means and eloquent speech, exhort and entice various spiritual friends to cultivate meritorious deeds and go to the presence of the Buddha to attend upon and make offerings, this is indeed difficult.
"If there are sentient beings who, possessing abundant merit and wisdom, are born in the Buddha-lands and are able to perform various kinds of Buddha-works of adornment, this is difficult.
If there are sentient beings who, within the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the Unsurpassed Vehicle, desire to seek liberation, this is truly difficult."

At that time, the Elder Mahābala expounded for our sake the teachings on worldly phenomena, up to those concerning the three vehicles and various difficult matters; although we heard them, none of us attained clear understanding. Each of us aspired to draw near to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—who possesses great supernormal powers and is endowed with all-knowledge—and we prayed: "We only pray that, out of compassion, you will extensively reveal and expound for us the wondrous Dharma of the three vehicles and various difficult matters. [Explain how] the physical forms, marks, and the five desires of human beings in this world are illusory and unreal, ultimately destined for extinction, so that all who hear may realize the nature of arising and ceasing, ultimately practice the holy path of the Bodhisattvas, and all give rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those elders, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"Good sons, you have skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding the wondrous Dharma of the three vehicles and various difficult matters. Physical forms are illusory transformations, and the five desires are not solid. Listen attentively and reflect upon this well. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma of the three vehicles according to the dispositions of sentient beings. Through skillful means, he reveals various parables to accord with their faculties and inclinations, so that they may believe, understand, and awaken, each gradually realizing pure nirvāṇa."

"If there are sentient beings who possess the *tathāgatagarbha*, whose roots of goodness in the Unsurpassed Vehicle have matured, and who, upon hearing the Buddha expound the Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, feel no fear or trepidation but instead cherish it with joyful aspiration; if their wisdom is clear and they practice with diligence, remaining firm and never retreating even when encountering adverse conditions or being oppressed and harmed by enemies, they will ultimately realize unsurpassed *bodhi*."

"If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured within the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and who, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the forward and reverse contemplations of the flow and cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, understand them clearly without doubt and develop deep faith and understanding; or, through the observation of the flourishing and withering of the four seasons in the world, awaken to impermanence and personally realize the fruit of sainthood."

"If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, they will, according to their respective understanding, know suffering, sever the accumulation [of karma], realize cessation, and cultivate the path; thus attaining the four stages and four fruits of realization up to the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa). In this way, regarding the three vehicles—whether provisional or ultimate, sudden or gradual—each according to the capacity and size of the sentient beings' faculties, they will joyfully practice and study, thereby distancing themselves from birth and death and attaining liberation and peace."

At that time, the elder Mahābala and the five hundred elders, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with joy; leaping for boundless delight, they praised him with one voice, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent, O Mahāsattva Bhagavat!

You are well able to expound the wondrous Dharma of the Three Vehicles. We now wish and desire to hear the unsurpassed Mahāyāna—the profound meaning of the Dharma, secret practices, various expressions, skillful means, and parables—which shall cause us to be free from doubt regarding the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, to give rise to deep faith and understanding, to practice with firm resolve, and ultimately to realize Bodhi without ever regressing or abandoning it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder Mahābala and the other elders, saying:

"That unsurpassed vehicle, the most supreme and profound Dharma, is the path practiced by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of great wisdom and great compassion; it is not a place where Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can find footing. Therefore, it is difficult for ordinary persons to believe and difficult for them to understand. You all should know this, join your palms, and listen attentively."

“Good son! If sentient beings abide within their fundamental nature and desire to practice the Unsurpassed Vehicle, they should give rise to great compassion toward all living beings, protecting and cherishing them with impartiality, and embracing them as they would their own teachers, parents, children, or kinsmen, regarding them with affection and pity. With a pure mind, they should provide vast offerings: seeing those who are naked, they give them clothing; seeing those who are hungry or thirsty, they give them food and drink; seeing those who are poor, they give them wealth and resources; and seeing those who suffer from illness, they give them excellent medicine.”

He practices the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) by nature, without being taught by others and without any stinginess, giving away beds, mats, bedding, fields, gardens, houses, exquisite treasures, flower garlands, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and all manner of offerings—even his male and female attendants and his own life—in order to advance toward bodhicitta.
"If one sees sentient beings who do not delight in the Buddha-dharma and do not practice the right path; who disparage the three vehicles and abide in false views;
who sever their roots of goodness and give rein to greed, hatred, and delusion;
and who commit various sinful deeds—such that at the end of their lives they shall fall into the hells and other evil realms, undergoing various sufferings without respite—"
These practitioners of the Unsurpassed Vehicle give rise to great compassion for those sentient beings,
cherishing and pitying them without regard for their own bodies or lives. They make great vows to dwell among those sentient beings suffering in the various realms of existence,
employing skillful speech to teach various dharmas, transforming those beings so that they resolve upon bodhicitta and continue their virtuous thoughts.
Disgusted with the retribution of suffering, they rejoice in the bodhisattva practices,
so that in the future those of like mind may cultivate pure conduct with firm resolve and without loss; furthermore, they offer wealth, food and drink, clothing,
their own bodies and limbs, as well as relatives, flower garlands, necklaces, couches, bedding, powdered incense, ointments, and all necessities of life.
Having realized that form is empty and the mind is free from attachment, they are able to relinquish all worldly desires and aspirations,
seeking for themselves the Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and furthermore, they successively transform all sentient beings, leading them to practice these supreme deeds together.

"If there are sentient beings who seek the Unsurpassed Vehicle with a mind free from inferiority, who firmly cultivate the *śīlapāramitā*, who possess great power of aspiration and maintain pure precepts—pure and untainted, without transgression—and who train progressively in the three types of ethical discipline; whose deportment is complete whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining; who subdue the three poisons and closely guard their sense faculties; who quickly awaken when demonic realms appear before them and do not give rise to attachment or delight; and who, even when encountered by evil persons or adversaries using forceful means to coerce or drive them away, remain established in right mindfulness."

Even if there should be an infraction, he has no mind of attachment; his actions of body, speech, and mind are free from fault and pure. He is able to study and practice all wholesome dharmas universally, benefiting all sentient beings while remaining far removed from harming them. Regarding the unmanifest precepts of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he never has even a moment’s thought of abandoning them, and he is likewise able to guard even the mundane wholesome precepts of humans and devas.

"If there are sentient beings who seek the practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle and cultivate the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), achieving its cultivation such that their anger is slight and their nature is naturally supple, they bring great benefit to all sentient beings. Even when encountering enemies who revile, strike, or slander them with harsh words, these practitioners do not give rise to resentment or anger, but joyfully endure it;
or when beset by the afflictions of cold, heat, poverty, illness, and exhaustion, they calmly accept all such sufferings for the sake of attaining Bodhi."

Even if there should be an evil person who intends to plot harm against them, or further insults and afflicts their body and life, this practitioner observes that all sentient beings are dependently originated, illusory existences that perish in each moment; seeing no sentient being at all, but only empty phenomena, they do not give rise to a mind of retaliation or malice.

"If there are sentient beings who seek the Unsurpassed Vehicle and, desiring to accomplish the *vīrya-pāramitā*, courageously and diligently seek the sublime Dharma of a bodhisattva—beginning from the initial arousal of the great bodhicitta and the practice of all correct conducts—never retreating or becoming indolent even when encountering adverse conditions; and though afflicted by the competing harms of the enemies of the *kleśas*, they don the armor of diligence to resist and subdue them, their minds remaining ever courageous and free from any fear, steadfastly persevering without regression throughout the long course of time."

"If there are sentient beings who seek the Unsurpassed Vehicle and practice the perfection of dhyāna with tranquility, their distracted thoughts will cease and right mindfulness will manifest; their body and mind will become harmonious and supple, swiftly departing from the hindrances and defilements of heaviness and agitation, and the bliss of pliancy and correct wisdom will appear."

"If there are sentient beings who seek the Unsurpassed Vehicle, whose minds are naturally sharp and intelligent, whose natures are capable of practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, whose wisdom is clear and discerning regarding the true and the false, who skillfully employ expedient means to guide others and adeptly distinguish between the causes and effects of the heterodox and the orthodox, and whose ignorance, dullness, obscurations, and defilements are slight."

"If there are sentient beings who, seeking the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, maintain a mind that is always equanimous, free from the distinctions between enemies and kin, and does not give rise to discrimination."
If one sees sentient beings practicing generosity or not practicing generosity, the mind remains free from attachment or aversion.
If one sees sentient beings guarding pure precepts or violating them, likewise there is no attachment or aversion.

If one sees sentient beings practicing patience or lacking patience, practicing diligence or lacking diligence, cultivating meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) or not cultivating them, possessing clear wisdom or being dull-witted and ignorant—regarding such classes of sentient beings, one remains free from the marks of discrimination and devoid of love or hatred. One regards them with equality, whether high or low, realizing that these phenomena are fundamentally without distinction, being of one *dharmadhātu* and having no separate self-nature. This is the meaning of the Mahāyāna, the supreme Bodhi, and the perfect, wondrous wisdom of all Tathāgatas.

"If there are sentient beings who give rise to even a single thought of faith in the Unsurpassed Vehicle, or even so much as resolve their minds to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are said to be Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of 'heading toward the abode of the Tathāgata.'"

At that time, the elder Mahābala and the five hundred elders, having heard this sublime Dharma spoken by the Buddha, were filled with joy and exultation, experiencing what they had never known before, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!
Please, for our sake, analyze and expound the essential points of the Mahāyāna Dharma, so that we may develop deep faith, understanding, and a joyful inclination toward its practice and study.

If there are sentient beings who, seeking the unsurpassed and most supreme Mahāyāna, do not spare their own bodies or lives, but relinquish their homes, wealth, treasures, and possessions, as well as their kinsmen, food, drink, clothing, bedding, and seating, flower garlands, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and all manner of offerings—may we now all vow to emulate those bodhisattvas, seeking the Unsurpassed Vehicle and practicing the path to enlightenment, not sparing our bodies, lives, kinsmen, or superior and exquisite jewels and means of livelihood, but practicing giving and making offerings, and performing the various *pāramitās* of a bodhisattva.
"We only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, will accept us and bear witness so that we may not forget or lose [this resolve].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Mahābala and the other elders, saying:

"Listen attentively! If there are sentient beings who, seeking bodhi and out of compassion for all beings, practice giving without seeking wealth or status, maintain precepts without seeking physical beauty, and practice patience without seeking followers; and who further cultivate diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—not for the sake of worldly saṃsāra or its causes and effects, but out of pity for sentient beings to seek the Unsurpassed Vehicle."

If there are sentient beings with sharp faculties and wisdom who thoroughly understand that the worldly physical body and the five desires are subject to arising and ceasing like illusions and transformations—possessing only provisional names but lacking any substantial nature—and who contemplate its physical characteristics as being a false combination of egg, womb, moisture, or transformation, appearing and disappearing like foam or bubbles, yet sentient beings, through their deluded thoughts, claim they shall dwell therein for a long time.

"Furthermore, one contemplates this body as being like a mirage, which has no substantial reality from the start; it arises from craving and is falsely perceived as water. It is also like a plantain tree, whose core is devoid of solidity. This present body is ultimately an illusion born of inversion—false, hollow, and fragile. It is like a vast wilderness, empty and possessing nothing; it is like a foul latrine filled with filth, with its nine orifices constantly discharging impurities. It is like a filthy well full of stench and evil, deeply loathsome. Furthermore, it is like an enemy or a venomous serpent, utterly unlovely. The afflictions of the five desires are like a torrential flood, drowning sentient beings and casting them into the ocean of birth and death, where they are submerged and transmigrate, with no foreseeable time of escape."

"Today you have drawn near to the Tathāgata to train in the bodhisattva practice; you have grown weary of and detached from the worldly afflictions of the five desires, and you recognize that the physical body is subject to decay and is entirely insubstantial. You seek the unsurpassed and most supreme Mahāyāna, gradually cultivating the various pāramitās, desiring to realize liberation—this is truly difficult to attain."
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of the Elder Mahābala, Volume One.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of the Elder Mahābala, Volume Two.
Translated by the Imperially Enfeoffed Master of the Dharma Bao Fa, of the Western Heaven (India), during the Song Dynasty.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānaśrī and others by imperial decree:
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Elder Mahābala and the other elders, saying:

“You have planted roots of goodness in past lives and possess firm faculties of faith. Desiring to study the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, you seek to subdue and sever obstructive defilements and realize Bodhi. You should contemplate those classes of sentient beings who, since beginningless time, have wandered through saṃsāra, maintaining bodies of karmic retribution through countless and limitless lifetimes; yet these physical bodies lack any solidity or reality, being like illusions and transformations.”

"These sentient beings, through inverted and deluded thoughts, construct the causes of karma; these are externally accumulated and brought to completion by various conditions, like water forming ice or a mass of foam. With the five aggregates and the four great elements as their basis, past karma serves as the cause that evokes their power; having accumulated all manner of seeds, they abide within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)."

When the parents’ mutual affection and union reach the peak of passion and joy, at the very end, each emits a thick essence—semen and blood—which is termed *kalala*. Consciousness initially takes up residence there; subsequently, as the semen and blood coalesce, the impurity solidifies and remains within the womb.

Throughout the various stages traversed, the winds of karma blow within, causing the physical features to develop; sustained gradually by the power of karma, the four great elements of the material body and the sense faculties become complete, while the mental consciousness and afflictions arise together with them.

Once separated from the womb and touched by external winds, painful sensations arise and cause one to cry out; one is unable to clearly perceive any objects. Driven by the conditions of wind, there is the movement of inhalation and exhalation; one drinks mother’s milk and produces excrement and urine. Mental consciousness manifests and gives rise to various conceptualizations; one indulges in various food flavors to nourish the sense faculties. There appear the physical form and its members—their beautiful or ugly characteristics—consisting of skin, blood, flesh, intestines, stomach, marrow, bones, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, mucus, saliva, excrement, and urine.

"Receiving various disparate retributions due to the causes of one's own karma, one is pursued by the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; one falsely gives rise to aversion or compliance toward objects that are enemies or kin; one indulges the mind in attachment to the forms and appearances of the five desires; and upon this body of karmic retribution, one further increases further karmic retribution—drawing close to evil friends while becoming negligent and disrespectful toward honored ones and kin."

Regarding bodhisattvas and the true Dharma, their hearts feel no affection nor do they partake of them; they indulge in folly to commit various evils, harboring anger, violence, malice, flattery, and envy, as well as resentment, strife, beating, and reviling, thereby harming and vexing sentient beings.

They give rise to perverse attachment toward the forms of men and women, like objects bound by rope that cannot be separated; they do not contemplate the impermanence of their own physical bodies, claiming instead that they will endure for a long time without ever perishing; and regarding various provisions and precious treasures, they seek to accumulate them excessively without ever reaching satiety.

“Defilements and impurities shroud the consciousness; one fails to cultivate wisdom and increases ignorance. One does not realize that the physical forms of men and women in the world, as well as those arising from the five faculties and the four great elements of one’s own body, are all defiled. Due to inverted conditions, one falls into impure states. Skin, blood, flesh, hair, fur, nails, and teeth originally lack any inherent self-nature; they are produced from the bonds of craving and karmic deeds. The causes and conditions for transmigrating through saṃsāra are never severed; the bitter fruits of birth and death never cease for even a moment. The fires of afflictions and karma burn and oppress the body and mind, so that day and night there is never any peace or comfort. Foolish, blind, dull-witted, indolent, and negligent, one takes no pleasure in Bodhi and turns one's back on the Noble Path.”

They do not seek purity within the defilements of their own minds; their bodies are constantly arrogant and their hearts are haughty. They slander cause and effect and disparage the virtuous and good.
Regarding conditioned phenomena—which are illusory and empty—they neither perceive nor understand them. Such ignorant sentient beings dwell in the ocean of birth and death with no prospect of escape.
“O you elders! You should fully awaken to such matters:

understand that physical forms, precious objects, utensils, and male and female attendants exist only through the conjunction of provisional conditions for a brief moment; while affection for them may flourish, they ultimately return to extinction. The nature of the five aggregates and the physical body is entirely empty; due to various deluded causes, one undergoes diverse retributions, just like a person in a dream who experiences all manner of events, which upon waking are found to be empty and utterly non-existent.”

"Therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who aspires to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* awakens to and is liberated from all marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*). With hindrances and defilements rendered slight and wisdom made lucid, although they make great vows to go among the various realms of existence and receive diverse bodies, their mind remains free from inversion in order to transform sentient beings. In this way, extending throughout the lands of the ten directions, they accord with sentient beings to perform various deeds—through giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation; through skillful means, they gather in and benefit sentient beings, causing them to abandon families of false views and enter the right path, cultivating all virtuous practices to proceed together toward the Great Vehicle, reaching as far as Bodhi without ever pledging to retreat or yield."

“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, attains the four dhāraṇīs through the purity of body and mind. Regarding names, phrases, and meanings, they attain the seal of patience (kṣānti-mudrā) and, without forgetting, contemplate them with precise discernment, thereby penetrating the true intrinsic nature of all phenomena.”
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with body and mind purified, impartially sustain all sentient beings, giving rise to no discrimination between enemies and kin, or hatred and love.”
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with body and mind pure, do not cling to the exquisite delicacies of the world, but partake solely of the flavor of the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna.”
“The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with body and mind purified, contemplates all conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing in the world as being entirely false and devoid of reality.”

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with body and mind pure, provide filial support to their parents and show reverent obedience to their teachers and elders; they receive their instructions without any thought of disparagement or arrogance.”
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with body and mind purified, are born into noble lineages as great kings; they transform the people through the True Dharma and bring an end to strife and contention.”

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess purity of body and mind; they remain far removed from those who commit violence and harm, such as butchers and executioners, and from all evil modes of livelihood and the conduct of outcastes (caṇḍāla). Having few desires and being content, they do not take what is not given, and they constantly cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya), severing all hearts of lustful attachment.”

“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses purity of body and mind; his speech is truthful and free from falsehood, his voice is clear and resonant so that all delight in hearing it, and he preaches the Dharma like a flowing spring, uninterrupted.”

"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with body and mind pure, is well able to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion; his mind is not stained by attachment to the fruits of the three realms of existence, yet he does not abandon the requisites for the dharma of suffering; wisdom manifests before him, and his mind is always clear and lucid."

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with body and mind pure, practice the four immeasurables and the six perfections day and night; even over a long period of time, they do not experience the slightest weariness, and for each of the eighty-four thousand afflictions and defilements, they cultivate corresponding merits as antidotes.”

“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with body and mind pure, neither clings to bodhi nor loathes arising and ceasing; having attained mastery of mind over all dharmas, they may either enter the cycle of transmigration or realize nirvāṇa.”

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with body and mind purified, develop deep love and joy for this most supreme Mahāyāna taught by the present Buddha; they are able to recollect the profound sūtras of the Buddhas of the past, upholding them without forgetting, and are also able to proclaim and turn the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas, like the flow of a great river that pours forth inexhaustibly."

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess purity of body and mind; they remain far removed from deceit, crookedness, pride, envy, and the conduct of wild beasts, venomous insects, and piśācas, and they treat sentient beings with loving-kindness, never giving rise to harm or affliction.”

“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with body and mind pure, does not covet material requisites nor dwell on food and drink; yet he does not abandon the poor and the destitute. In whatever place he is born, his resources and wealth are abundant, his retinue is accomplished, his physical form is upright and handsome, and he possesses great majestic virtue.”

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with body and mind purified, possess full knowledge of all forms of pleasure and complete liberation from all forms of suffering. They clearly comprehend and are not disturbed by the presence of the many sufferings such as birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from loved ones, the failure to obtain what one desires, and encountering enemies. They contemplate all sentient beings and their physical forms as being like dreams and illusions, lacking any solidity."

“O householders, you should understand according to what you have heard: the great bodhisattvas possess pure body and mind; the physical body composed of the four great elements and five aggregates is but an empty collection, ultimately unreal.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Elder Mahābala and the others, saying: "Good sons!

Such Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, within the realm of birth and death, take their cherished bodies as a condition for sentient beings; they manifest physical forms without any longing, remain free from attachment amidst various objects, and maintain equanimity of body and mind, neither grasping nor rejecting. They constantly perform virtuous deeds to bring benefit, peace, and happiness, never wearying or ceasing in their efforts to nourish and benefit sentient beings. Their lifespans within the triple world may increase or decrease according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, acting in accordance with them so that they may attain awakening, while their own minds remain free of desire."

“Regarding all sentient beings, he views them with impartial equanimity; and as for the most excellent and precious jewels among worldly things—treasuries of gold and silver, wealth, grain, clothing, food and drink, beds, couches, bedding, ointments, powdered incense, flower garlands, necklaces, female attendants, retinues, and all the various kinds of exquisite ornaments in the world—as well as his own physical body and life-span, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has no attachment whatsoever.”

"If there are sentient beings who come to beg for wealth, grain, gold, silver, or treasures from the storehouses; clothing, food and drink, beds, bedding, ointments, powdered incense, flower garlands, or necklaces; or even sons, daughters, male and female attendants, inner and outer kinsmen, physical bodies, or life spans—I am able to relinquish all of these, never having entertained a thought of stinginess for even a single moment."

Why is this? Because these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have long since realized that all things are illusory; they are free from attachment to the marks of arising and ceasing. Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās and reach the further shore, they deliver sentient beings so that they too may transcend the limits of suffering.

Therefore, regarding these illusory marks of the causal conditions of arising and ceasing, one seeks only to remain detached from them; because there is no mind of grasping or attachment, there is no stinginess. "Good son!

It should be known that when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus practices these subtle and supreme deeds of the six pāramitās, exerting diligence over a long period without even the slightest indolence, they shall swiftly achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, eternally conforming to the true and constant, with a mind free from regression.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the elders, reiterated this meaning and spoke in verse:
“Excellent, O elders! You should know this: these bodhisattvas, regarding the phenomena of arising and ceasing, [manifest] various bodily forms and various lifespans.”
Adornments, court ladies, and retinues— all these things he does not love or cling to,
for the sake of fulfilling the six pāramitās, transforming sentient beings, and leading them far beyond the limits of suffering.
"You, son of good family!
Listen with joy and attentiveness. You should diligently cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva;
do not allow yourself to be bound day and night by the fetters of afflictions such as greed and hatred."
Falling into the three miserable realms, there is no rest.
You, son of good family!
This body is like a vessel for food and drink; between its interior and exterior, it is [impure].
Always keep it pure, so that no evil or poisonous things may enter within.
Add various superior flavors; if anyone drinks or eats this, it shall not damage their physical body or their life-span.
Furthermore, if there be within the body greed, hatred, delusion, and the like—
The poisonous medicine of afflictions mingles with the flavors of all dharmas;
when sentient beings drink and consume it, they damage their Dharma-body as well as their life of wisdom.
"O son of good family!
All sentient beings, since beginningless time, have possessed but little wisdom;
they are like infants who think only of milk and food, having no other knowledge or vision."
Regarding the various characteristics of objects, one is unable to discern them;
there arise the faults of birth and cessation, where causes evoke effects, and effects in turn create causes, such that wisdom does not manifest before one.
The mind is perpetually dull and dark, craving only food and drink;
it nourishes the four great elements and dwells constantly in a dream, lacking any awakening.
Regarding the Buddha’s teachings, the mind makes no effort to cultivate them, like a drunken man whose words lack meaning or substance.
Regarding the objects of the five desires, they have never been distanced; day and night, with perverse thoughts, they only increase their suffering and affliction.
As sorrow and anxiety accumulate, body and mind become negligent;
they follow the current of ignorance into the ocean of birth and death, drifting, sinking, and drowning.
Receiving the retributions of various karmas, they suffer from hunger, cold, and affliction;
emaciated and haggard, they remain far from the further shore and cannot attain liberation.
Since time immemorial, within one's own true mind, it has been obscured by defilements and delusions, preventing awakening;
therefore, regarding illusory phenomena, one becomes greedily attached and stained.
"O you elders! There is nothing solid;
it is solely through the power of karma that one creates and gathers [the causes], revolving in the cycle of birth and death, receiving various retributions, and circling through distant eons."
There is no time for liberation.
Ordinary people, being ignorant and deluded, do not contemplate impermanence;
they are attached to self and others, intent only on their own ease and pleasure, do not associate with virtuous friends, and construct their own karmic conditions.
When the body perishes and life ends, one shall fall into hell;
transmigrating through the three realms, one undergoes all manner of suffering and affliction, as great fires press upon the body, leaving no place to flee or hide.
The great compassion of all Buddhas takes pity upon the world; yet for those who lack faith themselves, it is difficult to provide rescue or protection.
There is nothing real here; everything is merely gathered together through the causes of karma.
The sense faculties, objects, and primary elements combine and accumulate; this is conventionally designated as a "body.
Like foam or a bubble, it ultimately lacks any substantial essence. Since it is nothing but pus, blood, and decay, what is there to love or cling to?
Therefore, you should know that within this aggregate, one should practice the contemplation of impurity and give rise to profound weary detachment;
proceed toward the indestructible body, distance oneself from all evils, draw near to virtuous friends, believe in the Supreme Vehicle,
cultivate the practices of enlightenment, and extensively develop merit and wisdom.
Born in the Buddha-lands, their bodies and minds are peaceful and joyful,
pure and fearless. With exquisite garments, superior food and drink, couches and bedding,
flower garlands and necklaces, priceless precious incense, and various kinds of requisites—
With abundance and no lack, with a pure mind, I joyfully make offerings.
With a sense of shame and resolute conviction, I aspire to eliminate sinful karma and increase merit and wisdom.
Such a person, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, will give rise to faith and understanding in the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
gradually awakening to the true nature of ultimate emptiness,
which is primordially quiescent, as still as the ocean, without increase or decrease.
Though encountering the condition of wind, water forms waves; yet the waves are themselves the water, for motion and stillness share a single source.
One will not be born into the evil realms, gradually ceasing the cycle of saṃsāra, throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis.
For nayutas of kalpas, having clearly realized the ground of the mind, the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—
the causes of karma— no longer manifest; the various fruits of suffering are naturally not experienced,
and the physical body remains firm throughout immeasurable time.
Joyful and happy, they constantly contemplate inverted realms; skillfully expounding the essentials of the Dharma, they benefit sentient beings.
They themselves practice without illness and cause others to do likewise.
Tranquil, harmonious, and compliant; peaceful, secure, and joyful; deeply entering meditative concentration and free from all bonds of suffering;
always through virtuous conduct, they protect all sentient beings.
Not creating conditions for evil, they draw near to the wise;
they extol the Tathāgata’s most supreme and wondrous Dharma, reverently praising it and joyfully putting it into practice.
Observing all worlds, the conditioned phenomena of things are all like illusions and dreams;
not a single one is real. One thoroughly understands that food, physical strength, and lifespan are the very roots of affliction and suffering.

Not for a single kṣaṇa, nor even for a brief moment, do they cease; they relish various foods and drinks, which increases their faults, and though instructed by virtuous friends, their minds do not accept it with faith.
Encountering evil associates, they remain close and follow them, plunging deeply into ignorance and unable to awaken.
Regarding all sensory objects, they harbor deluded thoughts and attachments,
indulging in various diversions day and night without ceasing.
One develops a profound sense of weary detachment; furthermore, all worldly things—forms and appearances—are illusory and delusive, destined ultimately to decay and fall away.

Wives, children, and male offspring, as well as the conditions of one's kin and retinue, are like travelers meeting for a brief moment; when the causes and conditions of their karmic retribution are exhausted, they part.
The separation from those one loves cannot be avoided even for a moment; though they dwell together in mutual affection,
O elders, you should know that this illusory body is like a painter who creates various forms with colors— though beauty or ugliness may be produced, it must ultimately perish.
Furthermore, it is like the winter months, when accumulated water turns to ice;
though it remains firm and thick for a time, it eventually melts back into water. Why is this so?
The marks of form are illusory, and its essential nature is not real.
Through defiled attachment and craving, the mind becomes inverted;
thus one creates unwholesome causes, falls into the three miserable realms, and undergoes various sufferings throughout long kalpas.
There is no time of emergence;
even if one is born among humans or devas, one indulges in various pleasures, and through this illusory body, one commits evil karma without end.
Such deluded people are constantly afflicted by the fetters and defilements;
harassed by enemies and Māra, they remain bound at heart to wives, children, parents, and kinsmen, never once letting them go.
Day and night, they are entangled and constrained by these things.
Delusively regarding it as pleasure, it is in truth the cause of suffering; indulging unchecked in the three poisons, they nurture hatred and arrogance.
Such persons turn their backs on virtuous conditions and fail to give rise to wisdom, committing boundless acts of non-restraint.
Regarding their retinues— parents, wives, and children— as well as precious gems, food, and drink—
within these phenomena that give rise to suffering, their minds know no satiety; they do not contemplate renunciation,
but instead become addicted to and attached to them, seeking much wealth and treasure and amassing stores in their treasuries.
Seeing all those who are destitute and hungry beings, they lack a heart of compassion to rescue them from their distress;
they do not practice the Right Path, and as their wrong thoughts increase,
they cannot listen to or accept the instructions of the wise, and thus remain in saṃsāra.
"O you elders! Though the roots, stems, branches, and leaves are all lush and flourishing, they have long lacked moisture;
the soil is parched and arid, scorched by the sun, and its sap and essence are entirely exhausted."
Before many years have passed, it will surely wither and decay.
Though one’s prime years and robust complexion once filled the body, through attachment to the world and indulgence in the pleasures of the five desires,
the tendons and blood waste away, and one is invaded by the suffering of illness.
Their physical appearance is haggard, the faculties are withered and failing; unable to remain for long, they ultimately return to extinction.
Greedy for wealth and treasures, they do not know the distinction between sin and merit, nor do they contemplate impermanence.
Like a tree that has withered and decayed, it will soon be destroyed. O you elders!
Behold this illusory body, as well as those means of subsistence—gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.
Pearls and mani-jewels, conch shells and agates, coral and amber—these have no true substance;
they are like gathered foam. The deluded minds of fools falsely conceive them to be precious, thereby only increasing their greed and throwing their right minds into confusion.
Within the gates of the Buddha-dharma, there is nothing to enter.
The physical body and its requisites are all like things seen in a dream;
they possess no inherent characteristics whatsoever. Guard the six sense faculties and shut off the five desires.
Draw near to the Three Jewels and practice deeds such as giving; extinguish all stinginess and sever the mind of craving and attachment.
Contemplate those various desires as being like a great mass of fire that burns and cooks sentient beings—extremely terrifying and not to be clung to with longing.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of the Elder Mahābala, Part Two.
Translated by the Treasure-Law Master (Bǎofǎ Dàshī), conferred the purple robe,
during the Song Dynasty, at the Western Heaven (Xītiān) Translation Institute.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānaśrī and others by imperial decree, the Buddha told the householder:
"The accumulation of all phenomena consists of greed, hatred, and delusion; views, pride, doubt, and regret."
Regarding the objects of desire, they encounter them with deluded attachment, day and night,
without ever ceasing.
They do not examine the source of the suffering of birth and death, nor do they understand the world.
The characteristics of arising and ceasing have no intrinsic nature; they ultimately return to emptiness.
It is merely through craving that seeds are accumulated and formed; they arise provisionally through causes and conditions, appearing as if they exist through their conjunction.
When the force of causes and conditions is exhausted, they return once more to dispersal and extinction.
From fundamental ignorance, craving arises once more; as root and branch continue in succession like ants circling in a loop,
there is not even a fragment of a mind directed toward the supramundane,
the true principle, or the pure realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Delighting in and entering [samsara],
they drift and sink within the ocean of birth and death; deeply attached to the illusory appearances of the five sensory objects,
they are intoxicated, confused, and inverted, never awakening to the truth.
If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured, they will naturally draw near to spiritual friends;
their minds will constantly practice and cultivate the two benefits,
and toward those superior individuals who are able to preach the Dharma, they will [show reverence].
Giving rise to a rare and marvelous mind, one should love, delight in, and revere [the Buddha], never conceiving arrogance.

Regarding the Buddha’s merits—which are profoundly deep, subtle, and wondrous—and his inconceivable realm, one should be free from doubt and free from slander; likewise, one should not [be distracted] amidst the objects of the five sensory realms.
Delusive and false attachments arise from craving; by not committing various transgressions, one eliminates the causes of birth, death, and suffering.
One should increase all superior practices, cultivate the dharma of giving and other virtues, and always delight in reading and reciting.
In the Mahāyāna sūtras, one’s mind is free from deviant thoughts and devoid of divergent conceptions;
through the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna, one maintains pure brahmacarya, nourishing the dharmakāya and sustaining the life-force of wisdom.

They think only of food and drink, of the requisites for the physical body, and of the pleasures of the five desires, never feeling weary of them nor renouncing them. Not knowing the root of suffering, they do not seek liberation;
they cling to various non-Buddhist paths, harboring false perceptions and false thoughts, so that right mindfulness does not arise.
Lacking true wisdom,
if there are sentient beings who enter therein to bathe, play, and enjoy themselves,
such persons shall before long attain rebirth among the various heavens.
Thus, these deluded ones cling to various heterodox views; lost regarding cause and effect, they seek through error and falsehood.
Subverting the correct principle, they practice impure conduct;
with evil causes and bitter fruits, there will be no time of liberation.
"You all, O householders!
You should understand that the causes and effects of the world are a false conjunction, like a wooden puppet; whatever deeds are performed within them, [are likewise insubstantial]."
Do not give rise to arrogance; wealth and treasures in the treasury, honor, glory, and luxury are like things seen in a dream—they are empty as soon as one awakens.
Not knowing that these things are illusory transformations of arising and ceasing, and that their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent,
they cling to them in this world as being permanent.
Why is this so? Because since beginningless time, greed, hatred, and delusion have arisen;
bound by them and unable to let go, one encounters the agreeable and the disagreeable, joy and anger, without even a moment’s rest, amidst enemies and adversaries.
Constantly manifesting before one,
they attach themselves closely and draw near; together they form a source of entertainment,
increasing craving and becoming the cause of suffering.
Separated and parted from one another, they suffer grief, anxiety, and affliction; disputes and legal wrangling arise, along with their resulting resentments and knots of enmity.
Their physical forms grow haggard, their faculties decay, and their virtuous friends and kinsmen—
They all utterly despise and abandon [the Dharma], taking no pleasure in its practice; they do not contemplate wearying detachment.
As old age and sickness assail them, they harbor only grief and affliction in vain. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell.
Driven and rebuked by ox-headed demons, they suffer bitter and agonizing torments; without rescue or refuge, they wander through distant, long kalpas.
Their heads are like great mountains, their throats like the eye of a needle; they know not food or drink.
Skin and bone stand joined;
scaled, shelled, feathered, and furred—beings of water, land, and air, whether flying or crawling—seize and devour one another, constantly harboring fear and terror;
further encountering nets and traps, they have no means of escape.
Beaten with whips and canes, they repay their debts from past lives.
Or, if born among humans, they are poor and lowly, with impaired faculties and meager resources,
and are beset by many illnesses and sufferings.
When merit and wisdom are in discord, one’s accumulated wealth and resources cannot be enjoyed;
or, being prone to frequent anger, one constantly torments one's own mind;
or, afflicted by a chronic illness, one meets an untimely death.
That which they create is like a silkworm making its cocoon, binding itself;
like a moth longing for the flame, it ultimately leads to incineration. Body and mind are oppressed and distressed, finding no moment of peace.
Drawn along by evil karma, they wander to and fro without staying still.
In the three evil realms, they are like wandering through pleasure gardens; though they encounter manifold sufferings, they have no heart of regret or regretful concern.
They do not seek liberation, nor do they feel weary or desire to abandon [the state];
they undergo various retributions for their offenses—difficult to endure and difficult to bear—in a realm of profound and pitch-black darkness.
There is no place to which one can appeal; none among one’s entire retinue can take one’s place.
One must alone endure all calamities, passing from suffering into further suffering without any respite.
Such causes and conditions all arise from sentient beings’ beginningless ignorance,
which continues to manifest; through the fetters of greed and hatred, they move their bodies, speech,
and minds to extensively commit various evils, yet have not yet understood how to repent and eliminate them— the karmic causes for the three realms of existence.
Increasing moment by moment. O you elders!
You who delight in tranquility and aspire for liberation, with minds focused upon their objects of meditation—
The equality of defilement and purity will be naturally attained; karmic obstructions will become slight, and one will be far removed from saṃsāra and its various evil retributions.
Through faithful practice and cultivation, one gradually becomes able to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion;
one is also able to contemplate and fully understand that the physical body is like an illusion,
like a dream, like lightning, and like a bubble, for when sought out to its ultimate end, it has no place of true reality.
All wise people should thus carefully and thoroughly observe that both self and phenomena are empty;
yet within the true and wholesome Dharma of the Buddhas,
they should gradually practice sublime deeds such as giving, accumulating what is subtle and wondrous.
By increasing the sublime Dharma, one abandons the nature of ordinary beings and achieves the lineage of the noble ones.
It is like a mountain formed by the accumulation of soil, or like drops of water gradually filling a large vessel.
"O sons of good family!
Within the reality of things, you should cultivate deep patience and aspiration;
you must not relish or cling to worldly paths, but rather abandon false and illusory phenomena to realize true suchness."
Free from the suffering of birth and death, one attains the bliss of fearlessness.
Like a mirage, it merely deceives the deluded mind; it possesses no substantial nature.
Observing all phenomena in this way, their own characteristics, the mind does not fall into error.
Ultimately liberated, this is called the nature of the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Capable of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they practice and awaken in accordance with the various deeds and vows of the Buddha’s conduct; their minds never retreat or falter.
Exerting diligence over a long period, without any slackening or desistance, one is able to swiftly cultivate the six pāramitās.
Practicing the perfection of giving oneself, one does not hope for gratitude;
the three spheres are empty in essence, and both conditions are extinguished. Or, at a later time,
Free from all regret, with the faculties well-guarded, they do not transgress the precepts (*śīla*).

Even when confronted by adversaries, they offer no retaliation. Through the first, middle, and last watches of the night, they exert themselves with courageous diligence, remaining far removed from worldly entanglements and stilling all distractions.
Regarding the categories of good and evil, he possesses the power of discernment;
his physical actions are pure, and he constantly manifests restraint. His speech is gentle, harmonizing the minds of the multitude;
his mental ground is free from fault, and all discursive thoughts are severed.
All supreme, subtle, and profound dharmas, they are able to enter through skillful wisdom;
they gather in sentient beings and, according to their individual capacities,
preach with expedient means, causing each to awaken to and enter the gateway of liberation.

At that time, the elder Mahābala and five hundred elders, having heard this Dharma, were filled with immeasurable joy and exultation. They attained profound *dharmakṣānti*, the supreme *kṣānti*, and the unsurpassed *kṣānti* regarding the Dharma they had heard. They immediately rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the elder Mahābala and five hundred other elders addressed the Buddha with one voice, saying:
“World-Honored One!

From the past until now, we have never heard such a profound and wondrous Dharma. Today, at the place of the Unsurpassed Awakened One, the Possessor of All-Knowledge, the Bestower of the Great Dharma upon all worlds, we have been able to hear this wondrous Dharma. By means of this, we understand that all worldly phenomena are merely provisional designations, like illusions and dreams, ultimately returning to emptiness; thus, we have all awakened to and entered the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

May I, in a future life, be like the present World-Honored One, able to let out the great lion’s roar amidst immeasurable assemblies of devas and humans, manifesting the subtle, wondrous, and pure sound of the Dharma to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!
We now desire to speak verses in praise of the Tathāgata; we only pray that you will grant us your permission.
They then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
With a golden and subtle mark, most excellent and peerless,
you are able to expound the true meaning with a gentle voice;
having long cultivated the bodhisattva practices, your lifespan is immeasurable.
All sentient beings, upon seeing or hearing [him], are filled with joy.
A mass of pure merit, he dwells securely in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
like the Sun Deity who eternally abides in the realm of space.
All this is due to having practiced vast acts of giving in the past—namely, gold, silver, and precious jewels; elephants, horses, and carriages;
as well as heads, eyes, marrow, and brains; kingdoms, cities, wives, and children.
Being able to practice this difficult conduct, the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) is finally fulfilled.
By the power of their original vows, they manifest nirmāṇakāya and sāmbhogikakāya forms,
continuously for a long duration, exceeding the kalpas of the Gaṅgā River.
With inconceivable great compassion, you take pity on all who are blind;
you bestow the Dharma of ambrosia to remove their afflictions and bring them cooling peace.
For many eons, we have wandered through the various realms of existence.
Craving for material requisites, as well as for wives, children, and kin;
lacking merit and wisdom, they do not give rise to the bodhicitta.
They are stained by attachment to fame and to the pleasures of the five senses.
Through the auspicious merit of our past lives, we have fortunately encountered the World-Honored One;
having heard this subtle and wondrous meaning, we have realized that all phenomena are empty and illusory,
each attaining liberation, and our minds are now all at peace.
We pray that the Buddha will grant us permission to leave the household life and become śramaṇas;
may we vow that all sentient beings shall fully awaken to this Dharma-gate,
remain unattached to worldly pleasures, and swiftly accomplish the path to Bodhi.
At that time, after the elder Mahābala and the others had spoken these verses, each of them reverently sought to go forth under the Buddha, and the Buddha granted his permission.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, while still upon his seat, smiled with a serene joy;

through the power of his majestic virtue, he manifested great supernormal powers, emitting countless rays of light from the gate of his face, the colors of which were variegated like a multitude of precious gems.
Intermingled therein were what are called blue, yellow, red, green, purple, crystal-colored,
and golden-hued rays; the light they emitted shone everywhere throughout immeasurable,
boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds, reaching as far upward as the Brahma world— all of these...
The radiance of the celestial bodies and the light of the sun and moon were all eclipsed and could not manifest.
In the places illuminated by such light, no sentient being who came into contact with it failed to experience joy;
the karmic obstacles of beings with evil karma were eliminated, the blind were able to see, the deaf were able to hear, and the lame...
The mute are able to speak, the hungry are satisfied, the naked obtain clothing, and sentient beings in prisons are freed from their shackles;
all evils cease to exist as sacred realms manifest before them.
At that time, the great assembly of humans and devas in the gathering experienced physical and mental bliss such as they had never before known, and they all spoke these words:
"By what causes and conditions has this sign appeared?"

Each of them gave rise to the thought of enlightenment, rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha a hundred thousand times, and having paid respectful homage, made offerings, and offered praise, they withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, among the assembly, the Venerable Ānanda bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with a bowed body in reverent salutation, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions has this marvelous and auspicious sign appeared?

All those present in this assembly now harbor doubts, each thinking to themselves: "The World-Honored One never smiles without cause; that the Tathāgata has manifested this extraordinary sign today must surely have a reason."

Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, out of your great kindness and great compassion, we pray that you will expound this for us; for now the Buddha has adorned himself with various virtuous deeds, and the assembly desires to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"The Tathāgata has manifested this auspicious omen today because he wishes to proclaim the causes and conditions concerning how the Elder Mahābala and five hundred other elders have realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and will successively attain Buddhahood. You should listen well."

“Ānanda! These elders have, in the past, personally approached, made offerings to, paid homage to, revered, honored, and praised immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas. Having heard such supreme and true Dharma-meaning, they eliminated their karmic obstructions and distanced themselves from the three miserable realms. For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they were constantly born among humans and devas, experiencing superior and wondrous bliss; even until now, their wealth and prosperity are flourishing, they possess great retinues, and they are dignified in merit and wisdom, beloved and respected by all.”
"By the power of the roots of goodness planted in the past, they have now, in my presence, further heard this profound meaning of the Dharma. Ānanda!

This Elder Mahābala and the five hundred elders shall, in a future age, encounter the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya. In the presence of that Buddha, they shall again hear the pure and sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna, and will be well able to diligently cultivate the practices of the six pāramitās, such as the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving. They shall also approach, prostrate to, revere, make offerings to, honor, and praise immeasurable Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and shall likewise encounter all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa."

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, also proclaimed for them the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna; having heard it, they received and upheld it, and were further able to expound it in turn for others, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening immeasurable sentient beings.

“Ānanda! After this, for five thousand kalpas, the householder Mahābala shall be born in various Buddha-fields, practicing diverse forms of cultivation, encountering and meeting all Buddhas, serving and making offerings to them without ever doing so in vain. In the end, he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all shall share the same name: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Śrīgarbha.”

The realms of these lands are adorned, peaceful, secure, and prosperous; the duration of their True Dharma and Semblance Dharma, as well as the lifespan of their kalpas, are all exactly equal, and the number of people they deliver through preaching the Dharma is beyond measure.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda and the great assembly of humans and devas, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, so skillfully expound such subtle and wondrous Dharma and meaning, all praised him and further addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"By what name should this sutra be known, and how should we uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "This sutra is named 'The Mahāyāna Sutra of the Questions of the Elder Mahābala'; you should uphold it by this title."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, along with the bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and the Elder Mahābala, as well as all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
